newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo employees to be paid for first time in months.
newsitem.headline: Congo employees to be paid for first time in months.

text.p: Public employees in Laurent Kabila's new Congo are in for a shock.
On Wednesday they are due to be paid, many for the first time in six months, but one novelty comes with another less welcome: they might also have to work.

That will be a shock and a problem for the legions of civil servants who long ago gave up on the crumbling state of Mobutu Sese Seko's Zaire to scrape their living from second jobs, family hand-outs or even their wives' prostitution.

For Kinkela Pambu, receiving his $13 monthly salary for his office job will be a nice bonus. But having to go to the office and work may get in the way of his sideline, as an aide to an affluent Ghanaian businessman.

"As a book-keeper, I earn $70 a month. It's not enough, but it helps. I go to my office at Public Administration three times a week. I have some leeway. How can you expect somebody badly and rarely paid to work properly?" he asked, laughing.
The graduate, like many of his colleagues, relies heavily on his wife who sells cigarettes and vegetables to keep the household together.

Many of an estimated 600,000 civil servants in the nation of 40 million are more angered at getting only one month's pay from the new powers who overthrew Mobutu's 32-year autocracy last month, than pleased by being paid at all.
They also learned with bitterness on Tuesday that pay rises were out of the question, even though many domestic workers earn more.
"We thought that with the departure of Mobutu, things would change, but we are learning that our salaries have not been increased. It's a shame," Kinkela told Reuters.
Inflation touched an annual 900 percent in April but crashed to minus 20 percent in May, the month Mobutu fled with the cronies accused of helping him rob the country of its riches.
The currency has also strengthened well, but Jose Katamba, who works at the foreign ministry, said he was not optimistic his financial plight would improve any time soon.

"I can't make ends meet. My wife does not work. I have to pay all the family bills. It's a permanent nightmare," he said, adding that he was also a fairly unsuccessful "small-scale businessman" with his uncle.
"We sell cold drinks, but it's not working as we expected. We are deep in debt."

Katamba said that one of his two children could not go to school any more because he was unable to meet the tuition fees. Free schooling and health care are pipe dreams in Africa's third largest country that Kabila renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
"Food is a daily problem. What we eat, if we can, is poor in quality. We can't afford the luxury of eating everyday. It's too expensive," Katamba said.

Finance minister Mawapanga Mwana Nanga said last week that the civil servants who do not work will be laid off en masse as part of government efforts to restore order to a sector full of "fictitious workers".
How the heavily indebted state, which receives next to no tax revenue from a chaotic society, will be able to pay up on Wednesday is unclear. They say they will not print new money.
Some wives of state workers are widely believed to "misbehave" with the consent of their husbands who are constantly out of money.
Many civil servants wear second-hand clothes, the best they can afford. Some cannot even afford to take a bus to work.

Decades of economic indiscipline ruined what could have been one of Africa's richest states. Mobutu is said to have stashed away billions of dollars and to have enriched his followers at the expense of the population.
"The future is still bleak. Mobutu is out, but we still have a long way to go. The new masters are saying that the coffers are empty, but we've been waiting for ages in vain," Kinkela said sadly.
He predicted turmoil from Wednesday on, as civil servants were expected to throng into a crumbling Public Administration building in Kinshasa city centre to collect their low wages.
